#7534. Department of Justice Announces Nearly $150 Million to Hire Over 1,000 Law Enforcement Officers and Deputies

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Through the Office of Community Oriented Policing Services (COPS Office), the Department of Justice today announced it has awarded nearly $150 million under the 2026 COPS Hiring Program (CHP). CHP is a competitive grant program that provides funding directly to state, local, tribal, and territorial law enforcement agencies to pay for the entry-level salaries and fringe benefits of newly hired and rehired full-time sworn officers/deputies to make America safe again.

CHP is a flagship program in the COPS Office, which has a long history of promoting police partnerships. Through CHP, this Administration supports our nation’s front-line heroes by providing them with needed resources and expertise to enhance policing strategies and tactics. The express purpose of CHP is crime reduction through effective common-sense policing.

“Under the leadership of President Trump, violent crime has cratered to record lows,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “We were honored to host President Trump at the Department of Justice today to announce, among other actions, $150 million in grants for state and local law enforcement through the COPS Hiring Program. These funds will put more officers on the beat and keep the American people safe.”

The CHP program focuses on advancing administration priorities. Funding was prioritized for agencies that focused on: Violent Crime, Squatting and Encampment Enforcement, Homeland and Border Security, Nuisance Abatement and Quality of Life, School-Based Policing, and Combating Domestic Terrorism. Additional priority consideration was given to agencies that commit to ending deadly sanctuary city polices, agencies that participate in the Homeland Security Task Force, and agencies that are within rural jurisdictions.

Of the selected law enforcement agencies, one hundred and fifty-three recipients will use the funding to focus on violent crime, 40 will focus on school-based policing, 36 will seek to address nuisance abatement and quality of life, 17 will focus on other innovations in common sense policing, 16 will focus on homeland security and seven will focus on squatting and encampment enforcement.

The demand for CHP funding remains extremely high among law enforcement agencies nationwide. The COPS Office received 551 requests for funding and was able to award 269 agencies, approximately 49%. More information on the 2026 CHP awards can be found here https://cops.usdoj.gov/chp-award.

The COPS Office is the component of the U.S. Department of Justice responsible for advancing the practice of community policing and the Administration’s priority of Making America Safe Again by supporting the nation’s state, local, territorial, and Tribal law enforcement agencies through information and grant resources. To date, the COPS Office has been appropriated more than $21 billion to advance community policing including grants awarded to more than 13,000 state, local, and Tribal law enforcement agencies to fund the hiring and redeployment of more than 141,000 officers.

#7532. Calls for court packing fail the test of history

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Each weekday, we present news articles and commentary related to the Supreme Court in a smart, approachable way.

Free readers receive the Friday edition. Full access is for members.

A written companion to Advisory Opinions, bringing together each episode’s key arguments, takeaways, show notes, and source material on the Supreme Court, the Constitution, and the law.

Coverage and analysis of Supreme Court opinion announcements.

Professor Akhil Reed Amar, joined by co-host Andy Lipka, offers weekly in-depth discussions on the most urgent and fascinating constitutional issues of our day.

Divided Argument is an unscheduled, unpredictable Supreme Court podcast hosted by Will Baude and Dan Epps.

Please note that SCOTUS Outside Opinions constitute the views of outside contributors and do not reflect the opinions of SCOTUSblog or its staff.

As Democrats have taken control in Congress, we can expect calls for court packing to intensify. One especially prominent proposal has been to expand the court to 13 justices. In the last few months, we have seen former Vice President Kamala Harris say the Supreme Court should be increased to this number. In August, Rep. James Clyburn, a longtime Democratic leader in the House, endorsed this proposal on “Meet the Press.” Just in the past few weeks, Hillary Clinton said the party “should seriously look at expanding the court while the Democrats are in power.” Potential presidential candidate Pete Buttigieg has advocated increasing the number of justices to 13 as well.

Some of these calls come with superficially plausible justifications. Take Hillary Clinton’s proposal, for instance. “It used to be that you’d have one justice for each circuit,” Clinton explained. “We now have 13 circuits, we should have 13 justices.” Buttigieg has also argued for modifying the size of the court on that basis. But the symmetry argument is pretextual: It is no mere coincidence that the reintroduction of a one-to-one justice to circuit relationship under Democratic control would produce exactly the four seats needed to transform the current six-to-three conservative majority into a seven-to-six liberal one. Such a proposal then allows advocates to cover their desire for change to the court’s size in the language of a seemingly neutral principle.

It is true that the Constitution doesn’t fix the number of justices. And changes to the court’s size have not always been made for partisan reasons. In many cases there have been administrative and logistical needs that made changes to the size of the court practically useful, and even necessary. For that reason, we do not oppose changing the court’s size as such. Rather, we only oppose court packing, which we define as changing the court’s size for partisan reasons.

As we argue in a recent paper, and as already noted above, a key distinction when evaluating proposed changes to the court’s size is whether that change is constrained by some sort of even-handed principle or whether the change is driven by partisan advantage. Throughout American history, legitimate changes to the court’s size have answered practical problems, such as those accompanying the logistics of circuit-riding. A defining feature of court packing, by sharp contrast, is that it changes the court’s size primarily to benefit a particular political coalition without recourse to some prior rule or norm.

Political coalitions can always claim a pretextual justification for adding justices, allowing the political benefit to be presented as secondary to pressing administrative reasons. But the stated rationale for a proposed change cannot be enough to legitimize the change. Instead, a legitimate proposal must respond to a genuine institutional need. The grounds for change must, in other words, predate the political conflict rather than be identified retroactively to manufacture a justification for changing the court’s size.

The 13-justice proposal, from this historical perspective, utterly fails the test. The one-circuit, one-justice rule previously existed because justices actually rode circuit, traveling to hear cases in the lower courts. In those days each new circuit needed a justice to staff it. As the country grew westward, Congress added justices to staff new circuits (one in 1807, two in 1837, one in 1863). While, admittedly, those changes benefited the party in power, few treated them as a way to assert partisan control over the court.

But circuit-riding ended more than a century ago. Today the number of circuits has no practical connection with the performance of the justices. For example, when Congress carved the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit out of the 8th in 1929, circuits first outnumbered justices, and Congress did not add a seat. Nor did it add one when it split the overburdened U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit to create the 11th in 1980, and there were not calls to do so. And when the specialized U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit was added as the 13th Circuit in 1982, no one argued for a corresponding increase to the court. Rather, arguments for reestablishing the proportionality between circuits and seats on the Supreme Court have resurfaced only now after a string of decisions particularly unpopular with Democrats (most notably Dobbs).

Timing also reveals the motive behind these assertions. If the rationale for increasing the court’s size was merely or even primarily procedural and administrative, then there would be no reason to delay. But instead, as Clinton has stated, the court’s size should only be increased “while the Democrats are in power.” Nor, for that matter, have proponents named any administrative problem that four more justices would solve.

To clarify intentions let us explore a simple thought experiment. If Democrats believed the court needs four more justices, they could prove it by passing legislation to add two seats now, to be filled by President Donald Trump, and two more in 2029, to be filled by whoever wins the 2028 election. Accordingly, the court would get its 13 justices and achieve circuit symmetry. Democrats will undoubtedly not offer that deal, however, because under this scenario there would remain a three-seat conservative majority. This shows, of course, that the case for 13 justices is not, in fact, about the number 13 at all – it is about who gets to appoint the four.

Finally, history makes clear the consequences of changing the court’s size for partisan advantage. In 1801, lame-duck Federalists passed a law shrinking the court at its next vacancy in an attempt to deny Thomas Jefferson an appointment on it. The Republicans repealed this act, turning the judiciary into an object of partisan action and reaction, a conflict that culminated in the impeachment of Justice Samuel Chase in 1804. In 1866, Republicans shrank the court by attrition to keep Andrew Johnson from making appointments, defeating his pending nominee and leaving the circuit courts understaffed in the process. In 1869, with Republican Ulysses Grant elected, Congress set the number of justices at nine, contracting the court under a hostile president and expanding it under an allied one. Grant’s appointees then helped reverse a major ruling on paper money, a change that could arguably be seen as the product of Congress’ manipulation rather than constitutional reasoning.

The allure of court packing for partisan purposes will only continue to grow over the next two years. With Trump in office until January 2029, a Democratic Congress cannot expand the court on its own, so court packing will likely become a standard talking point leading to the 2028 Democratic presidential primary and the subsequent general election. As that debate continues to unfold, voters should remember one question to ask of these proposals: is the proposed change answering a legitimate, administrative problem with the court’s functioning, or is it a partisan reaction to the rulings themselves? Only the first should be understood as legitimate grounds to consider changes to the size of the nation’s highest court. Anything else risks escalating partisan retribution and destruction of the judiciary’s ability to act independently, a role that John Adams rightly identified as foundational for “the stability of government, in all its branches, the morals of the people, and every other blessing of society and social institutions.”

Jordan J. Ballor is executive director of First Liberty’s Center for Religion, Culture & Democracy.

Logan Tantibanchachai is a research fellow at First Liberty’s Center for Religion, Culture & Democracy.

#7531. Conservation group sues over seabird

The marbled murrelet nests in mossy cups on the tall branches of old-growth trees.

PORTLAND, Ore. (CN) â On the coast of Oregon, the marbled murrelet has long been seen diving into marine waters to forage for fish. But its population has declined, and a conservation group is targeting the Trump administration for allowing its forest habitat to be disrupted.

The Center for Biological Diversity sued the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and the U.S. Bureau of Land Management on Monday, accusing the agencies of failing to protect the birds from logging in western Oregon.

âThe Bureau of Land Managementâs logging practices are undermining marbled murreletsâ already slim chance of recovery in Oregon,â Lia Comerford, a senior attorney at the Center for Biological Diversity, said in a statement.

The Bureau of Land Management adopted new plans for almost 2.5 million acres in western Oregon in 2016. The plans were designed to increase logging and maintain protections for murrelets and other species that depend on mature and old-growth forests.

As part of those plans, the agency consulted with the Fish and Wildlife Service to prepare a 200-page biological assessment on the plans’ effect on marbled murrelets and their habitat. The service concluded the Bureau of Land Managementâs plans were consistent with the Murrelet Recovery Plan.

But two years later, the bureau modified its interpretation of those protections. The group says the bureauâs new interpretation differs significantly from the version the service consulted on and fundamentally undermines the serviceâs analysis of how the plans will affect murrelets and their habitat.

Specifically, the group says the interpretations made it so key protections are triggered far less frequently. The Fish and Wildlife Service then approved those reduced protections, in what the group called a âhighly cursory, incomplete, and arbitrary and capricious manner,â paving the way for logging in murrelet habitat.

Neither agency made the changes publicly available, the group claims.

âUnder the first Trump administration, officials at the agency went back on a promise to protect these precious seabirdsâ habitat,â Comerford said. âWeâre not going to let them get away with it.â

The marbled murrelet has been listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act since 1992.

The seabirds nest high in large trees in old-growth forests and fly up to 55 miles inland during breeding season from late spring to fall. Murrelets nest in small, mossy cups on large branches high off the ground, typically only in large, old trees.

Murrelets generally lay only one egg per year, leading to the species’ naturally low reproductive rate. Mated murrelets take shifts flying from the nest to the ocean to forage for fish while incubating the single egg. Marbled murrelets have high âsite fidelity,â meaning they often return to the same trees year to year.

Logging can displace breeding murrelets and lower nest success by removing trees with nesting platforms. Forest clearing can also increase predation. Crows, jays and ravens prey upon marbled murrelet nests and proliferate near forest edges.

According to the group, scientists have recommended a 300- to 600-foot buffer around occupied murrelet habitat for decades.

The Big Weekly Elk Project, which the bureau approved in 2021, includes logging in and around nesting habitat. The Center for Biological Diversity claims the bureau is ignoring murrelet protections and has already sold numerous timber sales under the project.

The group is asking a federal judge to find both agencies violated the Endangered Species Act and block the Bureau of Land Management from authorizing or implementing any logging activities.

âThe Bureau of Land Management has abandoned the protections it agreed to 10 years ago and is trying to maximize logging at the expense of these very imperiled birds,â said Comerford. âSadly, the Fish and Wildlife Service is just sitting on its hands, letting marbled murrelets spiral further toward extinction.â

The groupâs lawsuit follows the Trump administrationâs announcement of its intent to update resource management plans for western Oregon to increase logging.

The Bureau of Land Management declined to comment on pending litigation, but said it will continue to work closely with its partners to fulfill its public land and conservation responsibilities.

#7530. Dems ask SEC, DOL to not issue anti-ESG rules: Exclusive

A coalition of 17 blue state finance officials sent a letter to the agencies to counter prior assertions made by their Republican colleagues.

The Democratic finance officials took particular issue with the Republican officials’ letter relying heavily on a federal judge’s ruling against American Airlines in a lawsuit over the management of its retirement plans. The Republican finance officials used U.S. District Court judge Reed O’Connor’s ruling as evidence that the incorporation of factors like ESG is being used to pursue non-pecuniary goals.

The officials included state auditors, treasurers, controllers and comptrollers from New York City, California, Illinois and 12 other states who said that such a characterization of the use of environmental, social and governance factors is “incorrect and dangerously misleading.”

“The decision in Spence v. American Airlines, which dismissed long-term financial interests as a ‘mere pretext,’ fails to reflect the fundamental reality of long-term investing,” the Democratic officials wrote. “Fiduciaries are not speculators — they are stewards of trillions of dollars in assets that must sustain retirees for decades.”

Officials from Connecticut, Colorado, Delaware, Maryland, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Mexico, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont and Washington also signed onto the letter. They said that risks related to climate change, governance failures and systemic issues are “present-day financial realities affecting market valuations, insurance costs, supply chains and infrastructure resilience."

The Republican officials had said in their Jan. 28 letter that they held “serious concerns” that funds were being used to advance ESG or DEI goals and asked for rulemaking to prohibit plans from using assets to “advance political or social goals.” They also asked the Labor Department and SEC to issue comprehensive guidance explicitly saying that making investment decisions or proxy votes based on ESG or diversity, equity and inclusion objectives is “inconsistent with fiduciary duties.”

Connecticut State Treasurer Erick Russell called the request a “dangerous political proposal” in emailed comments to ESG Dive Wednesday, while Illinois State Treasurer Michael Frerichs went a step further, calling the approach “Orwellian” and “a reckless attempt to put politics ahead of sound financial decision-making” in comments Wednesday.

“Forbidding investment managers from assessing real-world risks — whether they stem from supply chain disruptions, environmental instability, shifting consumer demand, or any other factor — would restrict their ability to fully analyze investment opportunities and inherently runs counter to that fiduciary responsibility,” Russell said.

The blue state fiduciaries warned that if utilizing ESG factors in investment decisions was banned for fiduciaries, it could cause weaker investment performance, create greater exposure to market volatility and increase financial vulnerability for retirees.

“As stewards of public funds, we have a responsibility to ensure that our investments provide stable, long-term returns over periods of decades,” Delaware State Treasurer Colleen Davis told ESG Dive. “It is morally reprehensible and financially negligent to play politics with the American people’s retirement savings and investments.”

Acting SEC Chair Mark Uyeda and Acting Labor Secretary Vince Micone are currently in charge of two agencies who are defending a pair of ESG-linked regulations in court. Uyeda said last week he would seek a delay in arguments in lawsuits about the SEC’s climate-risk disclosure rule, indicating the agency as constructed is not inclined to defend the rule. A federal judge recently ruled in favor of the Biden administration’s Labor Department on its regulation allowing fiduciaries to consider ESG and other collateral benefits in the case of a tiebreaker. Experts expect that both rules are endangered under this Trump administration.

#7529. 11th Circuit tosses ex-Georgia Tech professor’s lawsuit against university auditors

The 11th Circuit panel found that the former Georgia Tech professor's racketeering charges stemmed from an independent investigation by state authorities, not a university audit.

(CN) â An 11th Circuit panel rejected a former Georgia Tech professorâs suit against two university auditors he blamed for his arrest in a racketeering case.

Chief U.S. Circuit Judge William Pryor wrote in a unanimous opinion issued Monday that Joy Laskar failed to establish that the auditors, Phillip Hurd and Patrick Jenkins, conducted the investigation that led to his prosecution. Laskarâs charges stemmed from an independent investigation conducted by state authorities â not the university officials’ internal audit or their report of suspected misconduct, the panel found.

âBefore obtaining an arrest warrant, Agent Vorrasi and McLaughlin conducted an independent investigation,â the George W. Bush appointee wrote in the opinion. âThey reviewed the same documents reviewed during the audit. They spent four months analyzing thousands of documents, deposing Sayana employees and consulting other university officials.â

Laskar was director of the Georgia Electronic Design Center, a research center where tech companies collaborate with researchers after paying membership dues. He was also co-founder and president of Sayana, a company that designed and developed high-frequency microchips.

In 2009, Georgia Tech began investigating a $600,000 shortfall at the center, according to court filings. Hurd and Jenkins learned during their audit that Sayana had billed the design center more than $1 million for the manufacture of prototype microchips which were later sent to a South Korean institute, which paid for the prototypes and research.

Laskar failed to disclose in conflict-of-interest reports filed with the university between 2007 and 2010 that he had a 42.5% stake in Sayana, according to the auditors. Sayana also did not pay membership fees to use the centerâs resources.

The auditors reported the suspected malfeasance to the university, which in turn sent the report to the Georgia Department of Law.

Laskar was charged in 2010 with two counts of racketeering, but a Superior Court judge dismissed the case four years later after finding the statute of limitations barred the charges.

Laskar filed a civil rights action against the auditors in 2018 in the Northern District of Georgia, claiming the government employees intentionally provided false and misleading information to law enforcement.

U.S. District Judge William M. Ray, a Donald Trump appointee, initially dismissed the case because Laskar did not receive a âfavorable terminationâ in criminal court, or a finding of innocence, which could maintain a malicious prosecution suit. The decision was reversed on appeal, but Ray dismissed it again last year after finding Laskar failed to support his claims that the auditors operated as law enforcement officers.

The 11th Circuit panel appeared skeptical of Laskarâs arguments during a hearing this month.

U.S. Circuit Judge Embry Kidd, a Joe Biden appointee, suggested the auditorsâ recommendation was no different from any other tip to law enforcement.

âSometimes investigations rely heavily on information provided by others,â he said. âThat does not mean that the decision by the investigator wasnât independent of the people providing the information.â

Pryor said it did not matter if the auditors provided advice and information to state authorities. The investigators specifically stated that their warrant application was based on their independent investigation and their own assessment of the evidence.

Pryor filed a separate concurring opinion Monday addressing the U.S. Supreme Courtâs decision in Thompson v. Clark, which determined a plaintiff only needs to show that a prosecution ended without a conviction to establish the “favorable termination” element for a malicious prosecution case.

Pryor defended the use of the common-law tort of malicious prosecution as the appropriate analogy for constitutional claims involving seizures pursuant to legal process, such as arrests based on warrants.

He distinguished those claims from challenges to warrantless arrests, explaining that the two types of seizures involve different legal considerations.

U.S. Circuit Judge Barbara Lagoa, a Trump appointee, rounded out the panel.

#7527. Trump administration withdraws application to Supreme Court to block lower court ruling on protected status for Venezuelan nationals

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Each weekday, we present news articles and commentary related to the Supreme Court in a smart, approachable way.

Free readers receive the Friday edition. Full access is for members.

A written companion to Advisory Opinions, bringing together each episode’s key arguments, takeaways, show notes, and source material on the Supreme Court, the Constitution, and the law.

Coverage and analysis of Supreme Court opinion announcements.

Professor Akhil Reed Amar, joined by co-host Andy Lipka, offers weekly in-depth discussions on the most urgent and fascinating constitutional issues of our day.

Divided Argument is an unscheduled, unpredictable Supreme Court podcast hosted by Will Baude and Dan Epps.

Originally published on Nov. 18; updated with latest developments on Nov. 19 at 4:35 p.m.

The battle over the Temporary Protected Status program – which allows foreign nationals to remain in the United States and work here when they cannot safely return home – returned to the Supreme Court on Wednesday afternoon. Specifically, the Trump administration asked the justices to block a September 2025 ruling by a federal judge in San Francisco that kept the program in place for Venezuelan nationals. U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer told the court that if they do not act, the order by U.S. District Judge Edward Chen “will spring into effect, inflicting severe and immediate harm.”

Then-DHS Secretary Alejandro Mayorkas designated Venezuela for the TPS program in 2021 and again in 2023. In 2025, he announced that the program would be extended through October 2026. Mayorkas cited a “severe humanitarian emergency” resulting from the “severe political and economic crisis” in Venezuela as the reason for the designation.

After Mayorkas’ successor, Kristi Noem, announced her decisions to end Venezuela’s designation and its subsequent extension, a group representing TPS holders went to federal court in San Francisco to challenge those decisions. Chen set them aside, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit upheld that ruling. In 2025, while that litigation was moving forward, the Supreme Court paused Chen’s order with regard to Venezuela, effectively clearing the way for the Trump administration to deport Venezuelan TPS beneficiaries while the case continued.

In June 2026, in Mullin v. Doe, the Supreme Court ruled – in a pair of cases involving Haitian and Syrian TPS beneficiaries – that courts generally cannot review the Secretary of Homeland Security’s decision to designate or terminate a country under the TPS program. Relying on that decision, the Trump administration asked the court to send the Venezuelan TPS case back to the 9th Circuit for another look, which the court did in October of this year.

When the case returned to the 9th Circuit, Sauer told the justices, and the Supreme Court’s initial stay of Chen’s ruling expired, the court of appeals entered an administrative stay, which is due to expire on Nov. 20. “Absent judicial intervention between now and” then, Sauer wrote, “the Department of Homeland Security will have to resurrect TPS status for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelans after a nineteen-month hiatus.” Indeed, he noted, his office “has been informed that the government could be forced to immediately release into the country some 1800 or so Venezuelan aliens from detention.” And all of this would result, he continued, even though the Supreme Court has already “conclusively held in Doe” that the TPS statute bars courts from reviewing the DHS secretary’s decision to designate or end the designation of TPS.

On Thursday, the Trump administration withdrew its application. In a letter to Scott Harris, the clerk of the Supreme Court, Sauer explained that “a few hours after we filed our stay application, the court of appeals issued an order” extending its current administrative stay (and therefore keeping Chen’s ruling on hold) until seven days after it issues a decision. “Should the Ninth Circuit enter an adverse judgment,” Sauer added, “we intend to immediately return to this Court for additional relief.”

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7526. Preparing for possible deportation, Mahmoud Khalil loses bid to get passport back

Khalilâs legal team argued he is âimmediatelyâ planning to apply for foreign visas but needs his passport to do so.

(CN) â Palestinian activist Mahmoud Khalil wonât have his passport as he prepares to make arrangements for his potential deportation from the United States, a federal magistrate judge ruled Monday.

Lawyers for Khalil â a green card holder who was detained for more than 100 days by federal immigration authorities last year for his criticism of the Israeli government â said he is âimmediatelyâ planning to apply for foreign visas now that he has a final order for removal. But they claim he canât do so without his passport, which was surrendered as part of his bail.

âThroughout this litigation and in other contexts, the government has repeatedly stated that Mr. Khalil would be able to self-deport,â Khalilâs lawyer, immigration attorney Kyle Barron, argued Monday.

U.S. Magistrate Judge Stacey Adams declined to return the documentation, however, finding Khalilâs request was âjust not specific enough.â

âIf the petitioner has a situation where heâs applying for a visa and that particular visa requires an original passport, you can make an application at that time,â Adams said from the bench at a virtual conference. âIt should be specific: âMr. Khalil is applying for a visa to depart to X country.'"

It is unclear which country or countries Khalil is seeking visas for. But Barron claimed that even his clientâs domestic travel has been hampered since he doesnât have a REAL ID or a driverâs license, either.

Khalil has been traveling the country on a book tour since he released his memoir, “No Land to Stand On: Notes from Detention,” in September. Because of that, he was also hoping the judge would agree to loosen his bail conditions. Khalil currently has his travel limited to the continental U.S. and must notify federal authorities of any travel plans 48 hours in advance.

Adams also declined to change those requirements.

âThe 48-hour notice requirement is really considered to be a very minor administrative requirement,â the judge noted. âIt is not very hard to comply with.â

Neither Khalilâs legal team nor the Department of Justice immediately responded to a request for comment on Adamsâs ruling.

Khalil was the first of several academics to be arrested last year in the midst of widespread pro-Palestinian protests on college campuses around the country. While pursuing a masterâs degree at Columbia University, Khalil served as a lead negotiator for the demonstrators, engaging in talks with the school to urge it to divest from Israel.

But President Donald Trumpâs State Department deemed Khalilâs advocacy harmful to U.S. foreign policy and revoked his green card on that basis, pursuant to a rarely used statute that allows the government to remove lawful permanent residents.

Khalil spent roughly three months in detention more than 1,000 miles away from his U.S. citizen wife in New York City, during which he missed the birth of his son. Last June, a federal judge in New Jersey ordered Khalil released on bail, ruling that he was neither a flight risk nor a danger to the community and thus shouldnât be detained pending removal.

However, after the Third Circuit reversed that ruling in January and the Board of Immigration Appeals issued a final administrative removal order in April â which Khalil is still fighting â the prospect of his deportation looms larger than ever.

In addition to his removal proceedings, Khalil is engaged in several lawsuits stemming from his unprecedented detention. He sued Columbia in September for purportedly failing to protect pro-Palestinian activists from harassment and doxxing. In July, he sued the Trump administration and Zionist groups under an anti-KKK law, claiming they illegally colluded to intimidate and jail critics of Israel.

He is separately seeking $20 million from the U.S. government as restitution for his detention.

#7525. Trump administration brings climate grant dispute to SCOTUS

Divided Argument is an unscheduled, unpredictable Supreme Court podcast hosted by Will Baude and Dan Epps.

After adding cases on President Donald Trump’s suspension of asylum for immigrants at the U.S.-Mexico border and the standard for securities-fraud lawsuits to the oral argument docket last Friday, the justices began this week by denying a number of notable petitions, including two DEI-related disputes. Then, on Wednesday, the Trump administration brought a familiar battle back to the Supreme Court’s interim docket, asking the court to address its effort to remove protected status from Venezuelan nationals. The administration withdrew that request on Thursday, however, citing a new lower-court ruling.

On Thursday, the Supreme Court denied a request for a stay of execution from Thomas Overton, who was sentenced to death for killing Michael and Susan “Missy” MacIvor and their unborn child in 1991. Hours later, Overton was executed in Florida.

Also on Thursday, the court denied a request for a stay of execution from Reinaldo Dennes, who was sentenced to death for the 1996 murder of Janos Szucs. Hours later, Dennes was executed in Texas.

On Wednesday, the battle over the Temporary Protected Status program – which allows foreign nationals to remain in the United States and work when they cannot return home – returned to the Supreme Court, as the Trump administration asked the justices to block a September 2025 district court ruling that kept the program in place for Venezuelan nationals. As noted above, the government withdrew that request on Thursday.

On Tuesday, the Supreme Court indicated that several notable petitions for review will be considered at the justices’ next private conference on Friday, December 4. The disputes address such issues as the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers and its approach to appointing acting U.S. attorneys.

The Supreme Court on Monday denied review in dozens of cases, including a clash between the Trump administration and University of California scholars over cuts to research funding; a California ophthalmologist’s challenge to diversity-related requirements for continuing medical education courses; and a dispute over Maryland’s ban on carrying firearms in “sensitive places.” It also invited the United States solicitor general to share the government’s views on a trio of cases brought against the Taliban by victims of terrorist attacks.

The Supreme Court Building will be closed for Thanksgiving on Thursday, November 26, and Friday, November 27.

The December argument session will begin on Monday, November 30. On Wednesday, December 2, the court will hear argument in Viramontes v. Cook County, on the constitutionality of AR-15 bans, at 10:00 a.m. EST. We will be live blogging that morning beginning at 9:30 a.m.

In a petition for review filed earlier this month, the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to weigh in on “its push to cut $16 billion in grants for a climate program, the largest grant cancellation case ever,” according to the Associated Press. “Democratic President Joe Biden’s administration awarded the money under a 2022 law to finance clean energy projects and accelerate the transition from fossil fuels,” but after President Donald Trump took office, the Environmental Protection Agency rescinded the grants. Groups that lost the money challenged this decision, and “[i]n August, a divided federal appeals court in Washington sided with the nonprofits and said the administration improperly terminated the grants.” “The administration has been adamant that nothing requires them to make these grants to these groups.”

On Thursday, U.S. District Judge Steven Merryday “allowed President Donald Trump to proceed with portions of his $15 billion defamation lawsuit against the New York Times and Penguin Random House LLC,” in which the president accuses the news outlet and publisher “of tarnishing his reputation with false stories about his business acumen before the 2024 presidential election,” according to Bloomberg. Merryday concluded that “Trump had sufficiently alleged ‘actual malice’ in connection with” seven “disputed statements, which requires showing that the authors and publishers knew the statements were false or recklessly disregarded whether they were false. It’s a high bar that must be met by public figures who sue for defamation, established by the Supreme Court decades ago to protect press freedoms.”

In a column for The New York Times, Nicholas Kristof described meeting with five men who were deported from the United States to South Sudan through a process known as “third-country removals” that has been embraced by the Trump administration and will soon be considered by the Supreme Court. The men, according to Kristof, “were nearly starving, can’t regularly communicate with their families or anyone else and don’t have any path to get to their home countries or, in the case of some of them, to ever see their American citizen children again.” “I hope the justices will take note of what has happened to those sent to South Sudan,” he wrote.

In a post for his Substack, Ed Whelan reflected on the potential reasons why Judge Cornelia Kennedy of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 6th Circuit, who was once described by a senator as “probably the most exceptional woman judge in the country,” was passed over for a Supreme Court nomination in favor of “a virtual unknown, Sandra Day O’Connor,” amid President Ronald Reagans quest “to nominate the first female justice.” O’Connor likely benefitted from, among other things, having “a powerful advocate” in Chief Justice Warren Burger, who “energetically lobb[ied] for O’Connor with White House officials and evidently with Reagan himself.” A comparison between O’Connor and Kennedy “offers lessons about the pressures and incentives that shape a president’s selection of a Supreme Court nominee,” Whelan wrote.

In a piece on the legacy of Judge Richard Posner, who died on November 10, The Economist celebrated his remarkable career, describing him as “a giant of American law.” Scholars told the publication that “Posner may prove more influential than many Supreme Court justices,” in large part because he wrote “more than 500 articles, 50 books and 3,300 judicial opinions on everything from the law and sex to how judges think” during his career. “We pay attention to the justices because their opinions matter, but very few of them have anything interesting or original to offer,” said Larry Kramer of the London School of Economics. “Dick Posner did.”

On Thursday, the Trump administration withdrew its request for the Supreme Court to block a lower court ruling that would allow Venezuelan nationals to participate in the Temporary Protected Status program, noting that the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit has ensured the ruling will remain on hold. “Should the Ninth Circuit enter an adverse judgment,” wrote U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer, “we intend to immediately return to this Court for additional relief.”

Time is running out for the justices to add cases to this term’s oral argument docket. Despite being short on time, however, the justices are not short on major petitions for review. Over the next two months, they will likely consider petitions addressing such high-profile issues as the Trump administration’s ban on transgender servicemembers and state laws requiring Ten Commandments displays in public school classrooms.

By Jordan J. Ballor & Logan Tantibanchachai

In a column for SCOTUSblog, Jordan J. Ballor and Logan Tantibanchachai reflected on Democrats’ recent embrace of court packing, which they “define as changing the court’s size for partisan reasons.” Such an approach to court reform “risks escalating partisan retribution and destruction of the judiciary’s ability to act independently,” they wrote.

In his Immigration Matters column on Wednesday, César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández explored what Democrats’ success in the midterm elections could mean for a challenge to an Iowa law criminalizing certain immigration-related conduct, Bird v. Iowa Migrant Movement for Justice. Because Iowa’s Republican attorney general lost her reelection bid to a Democrat, it’s now unclear if the state will move forward with its defense of the law, “providing yet another reason why elections matter.”

In his Courtly Observations column on Tuesday, Erwin Chemerinsky revisited the oral argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, during which several conservative justices appeared to suggest “that a law’s discriminatory effect against a religion should be a basis for striking it down.” Such an approach to free exercise would be at odds “with a half century of law under equal protection holding that disparate impact ... is not enough to prove discrimination,” Chemerinsky contended.

In her In the Interim column on Monday, Taraleigh Davis revisited comments made by Justice Samuel Alito this fall about the court’s emergency docket, including why it’s so busy these days. The data, according to Davis, “support part of what Alito said but complicate the rest.”

Sarah Isgur and David French discuss the nature of lame-duck confirmations after the showdown between Texas Sens. John Cornyn and Ted Cruz, journalists’ records, and weakening the presidential veto.

Akhil Amar and Andy Lipka continue their discussion on the significance of and fallout from this month’s midterm elections.

The Closer Look in Friday editions is typically a judicial biography. This week, we cover Justice Levi Woodbury, who served on the court from 1845 to 1851.

Being the first justice to attend law school and the first of two New Hampshire justices (the second being Justice David Souter) has not saved Justice Levi Woodbury’s reputation from “declin[ing] dramatically over the years,” as a “reputational study” of the justice published in the Journal of Supreme Court History put it.

Woodbury was born in December 1789 in Francestown, New Hampshire. As the eldest son, he faced immense pressure to succeed and was “near obsessive” about his education, according to Oyez. He attended Atkinson Academy before enrolling at Dartmouth at 16, earning money teaching in the towns around Hanover to afford school.

Woodbury then attended law school (the other justices had “read law” through apprenticeships or were self-taught), studying at Litchfield Law school in Connecticut. Per Oyez, however, his time there was brief: He quickly came to the conclusion that he “did not enjoy [law school]” and apprenticed instead before being admitted to the bar in 1812.

During the War of 1812, Woodbury drafted the Hillsborough Resolves, statements backing President James Madison’s decision to fight Britain (and arguing against Daniel Webster’s condemnation of the war). With this, Woodbury became “one of the few” New Englanders to support the War of 1812. While then clerking for the state Senate, Woodbury connected with Gov. William Plumer, who in 1816 appointed Woodbury, then 27, to the New Hampshire Superior Court (the state’s top court).

In 1823, the New Hampshire Democratic-Republicans faced “bitter factionalism within,” and a group of them (displeased with their caucus’ choice for governor) chose Woodbury as their nominee instead, helping him to become New Hampshire’s 15th governor by a significant margin. Woodbury’s attempt to reunite the party met with little success, however, and he was not reelected. Still, by 1825 Woodbury had become speaker of the state House and a U.S. senator and later chaired the Senate Committee on Commerce. During that time, Woodbury, who was sympathetic to President Andrew Jackson, supported the Indian Removal Act of 1830. He was subsequently appointed by Jackson in March 1831 as secretary of the Navy.

In 1834, Jackson shifted Woodbury to the Treasury, where he denied entrusting federal money to the Second Bank of the United States (like his predecessor, Roger B. Taney), instead giving it to commercial banks. In that position, he also issued the Specie Circular, which directed federal land offices to accept “nothing except what is directed by the existing laws, viz, gold and silver, and in the proper cases Virginia land scrip,” but not paper money, for land purchases. The Circular is often cited as a “primary cause” of the Panic of 1837.

In 1841, Woodbury returned to the Senate rather than serve as chief justice of New Hampshire’s Superior Court. After Justice Joseph Story died in September 1845, President James Polk nominated Woodbury as a recess appointment to the Supreme Court, and he was confirmed by the Senate that January.

In 1847, Woodbury authored the court’s unanimous opinion in Jones v. Van Zandt, which upheld the Fugitive Slave Act of 1793 as constitutional. Oyez writes that although “[m]any thought this indicated a pro-slavery stance … really his vote was motivated by an appreciation for states’ rights and a fear that the constitution was being interpreted too liberally.” Yet whereas Justice John McLean wrote that “the Constitution treats slaves as persons,” Woodbury “repeatedly referr[ed] to enslaved people as ‘property.’” One anti-slavery paper wrote that “if there be a man in the United States utterly heartless on the subject of slavery, it is Levi Woodbury” and that “[w]e know of no opinion on record of any slaveholding court, so inhumane in tone and language, as the opinion of Judge Woodbury, declared in the Van Zandt case.”

In 1849’s Luther v. Borden, Woodbury was the only justice to dissent, concluding that Rhode Island’s statute establishing martial law was unconstitutional. Under such a law, he wrote, the “whole population” was “exposed … to be seized, without warrant or oath” and that “[b]y it, every citizen … exists with, a rope around his neck.” Woodbury likewise dissented in 1849’s Passenger Cases, which asked whether a tax could be imposed “upon alien passengers” arriving in the ports of New York and Massachusetts. Woodbury wrote that the commerce clause did not give the federal government exclusive immigration powers, and that states could tax immigrants after they arrived in the state ports.

Woodbury also pursued his political ambitions while on the court. In 1848, John C. Calhoun said – reportedly influenced by Woodbury’s decision in Van Zandt – that he “would run best in the South.” Woodbury campaigned for president, but his apparent efforts to appeal to both slavery and anti-slavery advocates hurt his candidacy, and Lewis Cass ultimately received the Democratic nomination.

Although Woodbury “looked like a front-runner again for an 1852 nomination,” he died in 1851 in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, at age 61, and the nomination went to his former clerk, Franklin Pierce.

MR. MILLER: “– No, I think they mean what a district judge honoring his Article III commission concludes after an intensive evaluation of the entirety of the complaint, looking for that strong inference, putting on his sort of motion to dismiss 12(b)(6) hat, says okay –”

MR. MILLER: “– No, I did not mean that. Don't take me literally on that. For heavens sakes, I'm from Brooklyn. I'm very colloquial. I'm very sorry about that.”

JUSTICE SCALIA: “Let me write that down. We should not take you literally. All right.”

— Tellabs, Inc. v. Makor Issues & Rights, Ltd. (2007)

#7524. Federal judge says he can’t stop Trump’s ICC judge sanctions

President Donald Trump imposed the sanctions on judges after the ICC pursued investigations involving U.S. personnel in Afghanistan and Israeli leaders over the war in Gaza.

MANHATTAN (CN) âÂ A federal judge in New York on Monday said he doesn’t have the power to stop President Donald Trump from imposing sanctions on judges of the International Criminal Court in the form of frozen bank accounts, canceled credit cards and blocked travel.

Trump declared a national emergency in a 2025 executive order with respect to any ICC effort to investigate, arrest, detain or prosecute “any United States person” unless the U.S. formally consents or becomes a state party to the Rome Statute, which established the ICC in 2002 to prosecute war crimes and crimes against humanity.

Judges Kimberly Prost, Solomy Bossa and Reine Alapini-Gansou of the ICC turned to the U.S. courts asking to be removed from the sanctions list, unblock their frozen property and bar Trump from enforcing measures against them. But U.S. District Judge Jesse Furman dismissed all but one of their claims and denied a preliminary injunction, finding “deference here is owed not only to the president but also to Congress.”

“In short, whatever the courtâs own assessment of the circumstances may be, plaintiffsâ allegations do not permit the court to hold that the president acted ultra vires when he declared a national emergency to address what he determined to be an ‘unusual and extraordinary threat, which has its source in whole or substantial part outside the United States,’ to the national security, foreign policy, or economy of the United States,” Furman wrote in a 37-page order.

Each judge was sanctioned over a different decision. Prost, of Canada, and Bossa, of the Republic of Uganda, joined a 2020 appeals ruling that allowed the ICC prosecutor to investigate suspected war crimes and crimes against humanity in Afghanistan. Alapini-Gansou, of the Republic of Benin, sat on the panel that approved arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defense Minister Yoav Gallant.

The trio of judges sued under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act, U.S. Constitution and Administrative Procedure Act. Furman, a Barack Obama appointee, dismissed the due process and takings clause claims, but preserved the plaintiffs’ APA claim accusing the federal government of arbitrary and capricious sanctions designations. That count is premature, the judge said, since it must be decided on the full administrative record that was before Secretary of State Marco Rubio when he made the decision.

Furman noted there are three other cases in Manhattan federal court involving challenges to Trump’s executive order, but unlike the others, the trio of judges don’t bring First Amendment claims and are challenging the order in its entirety.

Those other, earlier lawsuits filed by U.S. human rights advocates resulted in rulings barring the administration from enforcing the order against Americans providing speech-based services to the ICC.

Trump signed Executive Order 14203 on Feb. 6, 2025, after the ICC pursued investigations involving U.S. personnel in Afghanistan and Israeli leaders over the war in Gaza.

After first sanctioning ICC prosecutor Karim Khan, the White House expanded its list to include the international courtâs two deputy prosecutors, eight judges, U.N. Special Rapporteur Francesca Albanese and three Palestinian human rights organizations: Al-Haq, Al Mezan Center for Human Rights and the Palestinian Center for Human Rights.

The sanctions formally freeze U.S.-based assets and bar Americans from providing funds or services. The judges say their effects ripple across global banks, payment systems and technology companies that rely heavily on the U.S. financial system.

âThe sanctions regime punishes Judges Prost, Bossa and Alapini-Gansou for having done nothing more than â when called upon to adjudicate matters before them â faithfully discharge their judicial offices by rendering decisions with which the administration disagrees,â the judges say in their lawsuit.

In addition to arguing that the sanctions strike at the independence of international courts by punishing judges for carrying out their duties, the judges say Trump’s order disrupts ICC investigations that Republican and Democratic administrations alike have backed over the years, including cases involving Sudan, Libya, Uganda, Mali, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Ukraine.

In June 2023, the court decided Students for Fair Admissions, Inc. v. University of North Carolina, holding that race-conscious admissions at Harvard and the University of North Carolina violated the Constitution. Chief Justice John Roberts’ majority opinion in the case, along with Justice Brett Kavanaugh’s concurrence, cited Justice Sandra Day O’Connor’s 2003 prediction in Grutter v. Bollinger that “25 years from now, the use of racial preferences will no longer be necessary to further” student body diversity.

But the justices did not account for one thing, according to Brooklyn Law School Professor Yuvraj Joshi: O’Connor’s later misgivings about that statement. In interviews with her biographer after she left the court, O’Connor acknowledged that the 25-year figure “may have been a misjudgment.” When asked for a new estimate, she replied, “[t]here’s no timetable. You just don’t know.”

#7522. Defense maintains star witness lied in ex-Oakland mayor’s corruption trial

Attorneys for former Oakland mayor Sheng Thao and her co-defendants have painted the government's primary witness as a liar who cooperated with FBI for leniency.

OAKLAND, Calif. (CN) â In a final hour Hail Mary in a nearly two-monthlong bribery trial featuring ex-Oakland Mayor Sheng Thao, the defense tried to call the credibility of the prosecution’s star witness into question.

But Chief U.S. District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers didn’t seem particularly convinced on Monday by a motion to dismiss the case based on what the defense called Mario Juarez’s false testimony.

âThe request is extraordinary,â the Barack Obama appointee said of the motion filed Saturday. âThis jury understands, as well as everyone in the courtroom knows, Juarez lies.â

Juarez, a longtime East Bay political player, claims he entered into a bribery scheme with father and son David and Andy Duong to secure city contracts for their shipping container homes company.

The Duongs, along with Thao and her romantic partner Andre Jones, charged with crimes including conspiracy, bribery, fraud and making a false statement to a government official.

All four co-defendants have pleaded not guilty. Thao faces a maximum sentence of 95 years in prison if convicted on all charges. Thao, Jones and the Duongs waived the right to testify in their own defense.

âHeâs a con artist, you did a very good job,â Rogers said referring to the defenseâs attack of Juarezâs credibility. âItâs not clear that the government is going to a get a conviction, or a verdict, period. This jury could hang.â

Juarez, who became an FBI informant reportedly after a falling out with the Duongs, testified he and the Duongs bribed Thao in exchange for lucrative contracts with the city to buy up to 300 container units and an extension of the Duongs’ waste management company, California Waste Solutions. Jonesâ supposed role included collecting the bribes for Thao through a âno-showâ job at the container home company, Evolutionary Homes.

Now in the seventh week of trial, David Duongâs attorney Jeffrey Schenk also questioned IRS Special Agent Christine Stegner about a spreadsheet she created to reconcile Juarezâs Evolutionary Homes expense reports to the Duongs, which included doctored bank records.

The defense had previously asked to suppress Stegner’s previous testimony for the prosecution about how she formulated the spreadsheet in connection to her interviews with Juarez and hearing his testimony in court. Before the 15-person jury was seated Monday, Rogers denied the request to suppress.

Stegner also testified she didnât ask Juarez about the doctored bank records, nor was she asked to do so by the prosecution.

The defenseâs second witness, Luis Mejia Solis, a parking lot owner in East Oakland, testified through a Spanish court interpreter that he knew Juarez because he stored two box trucks in his lot.

Mejia testified he accompanied Juarez in a black BMW in May 2024 to an Oakland Embarcadero building, the headquarters of California Waste Solutions and Evolutionary Homes. He said Juarez tried to use a set of keys to get into the building, but they didnât work.

Mejia said during the incident Juarez got into an argument with âan Asian man,â but then abruptly ran back to the car and hid âa black metal objectâ he pulled from the back of his waistband and placed under the driverâs seat, saying he needed to âhide the gun.â

Juarez testified earlier in the trial during the incident that Duong associates showed up after Mejia left and beat him up, taking his watch and gold chain after he was locked out of the Evolutionary Homes office.

Juarez had also testified that part of the scheme was his funding of $75,000 for negative mailers about Thaoâs mayoral opponents, in exchange for Thaoâs promise to help Evolutionary Homes.

Former Thao staffer Brandon Harami testified Jones was a volunteer during Thaoâs mayoral campaign and helped produce mailers for the campaign that were different from Juarezâs negative mailers.

âI thought it was very poorly done,â Harami told Jonesâ attorney Mark Goldrosen.

âYou know better than to edit peopleâs features, especially a Black manâs features,â he said, referencing a mailer against Thao’s opponent Loren Taylor.

During Hamari’s cross-examination, Assistant U.S. Attorney Abraham Fine pointed out that Harami wasn’t present when two photographs at separate events were taken of Thao in conversation with Juarez and Andy Duong.

The defense case rested by the end of day. Other court proceedings will continue Tuesday before closing arguments and deliberations begin next week.

#7521. Quebec politicians decry court-ordered oath of allegiance to King Charles III

Quebec politicians will have to pledge an oath to King Charles III or risk legal battles over their laws.

MONTREAL (CN) â The Superior Court of Quebec ruled Monday that a 2022 law allowing members of the province’s National Assembly to pledge allegiance only to Quebecers, and not to the British king, is unconstitutional.

The decision sparked waves of protests from Quebec politicians, putting the upcoming legislative session in limbo.

Superior Court Justice Ian Demers found the provincial government overstepped its powers by abolishing the king’s oath without the approval of Ottawa and the other provinces. He ruled in favor of Lawrence David, a University of Ottawa law professor who challenged the legislation in August.

The judge agreed with David that suspending the law is necessary to avoid chaos in the National Assembly. The professor and founder of the Public Interest Litigation Institute argued that laws adopted by members of the National Assembly who had not pledged their allegiance to King Charles III would be invalid and that the law violated Quebecers’ right to proper representation.

David also claimed the oath could be abolished only with the unanimous consent of the provinces and the federal Parliament, because the change encroached on the role of the lieutenant governor. Canada is a constitutional monarchy, and lieutenant governors represent the Crown.

The Legislature adopted Bill 4 in December 2022, after the three Parti QuÃ©bÃ©cois members elected that year refused to swear the oath required by the Constitution Act of 1867, and were barred from taking their seats in the National Assembly.

Quebec politicians appear to agree with the law. None of the 127 members of the National Assembly elected in October has sworn allegiance to the king. The court nonetheless found the law unconstitutional.

“The Constitution is not an Ã  la carte menu in which a subject complies with what suits them,” Demers wrote in his ruling. “Any other proposal would lead to constitutional disorder, or even chaos.”

“If the stay were not ordered, all laws passed by the National Assembly would be unconstitutional and would have to be reenacted,” he added, predicting the process would only “paralyze” the government and harm Quebecers.

Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon, Parti Quebecois leader â and former lawyer â denounced the decision.

“The government of Quebec strongly condemns a ruling that clearly goes against the democratic will of Quebecers, who have expressed their desire to put an end to the disloyal act of swearing an oath to the British monarch and to the straitjacket of the monarchy in general,” the premier said in a statement released on social media in French.

In a press conference in Montreal on Monday, St-Pierre Plamondon called the ruling a “disgrace” and said he “cannot take an oath to the king of England.” He vowed to take all necessary measures to oppose the judgment.

The premier noted Quebec never signed the 1982 Canadian Constitution, and that the Constitutional Act of 1867 was imposed on the French-Canadian people after the British conquest of the French territory. He insists Quebecers should be allowed to follow the democratic process rather than be forced to follow rules imposed on them.

The legislative assembly set for Dec. 1 is now up in the air. Lawmakers must decide between swearing allegiance to the king and risking court challenges to every decision they make.

All the opposition parties also criticized the ruling and welcomed the government’s appeal, deploring that the decision could push back further the start of the National Assembly.

The Parti Quebecois has long been fighting the presence of the monarchy in Quebec. St-Pierre Plamondon promised earlier this year to abolish the Office of the Lieutenant Governor of Quebec, or at least divert its resources to fight issues such as the homelessness crisis.

Courthouse News reporter Tatiana Mulowayi-Pelletier is based in Montreal, Canada.

#7520. Criminal law is constitutional law

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

Each weekday, we present news articles and commentary related to the Supreme Court in a smart, approachable way.

Free readers receive the Friday edition. Full access is for members.

A written companion to Advisory Opinions, bringing together each episode’s key arguments, takeaways, show notes, and source material on the Supreme Court, the Constitution, and the law.

Coverage and analysis of Supreme Court opinion announcements.

Professor Akhil Reed Amar, joined by co-host Andy Lipka, offers weekly in-depth discussions on the most urgent and fascinating constitutional issues of our day.

Divided Argument is an unscheduled, unpredictable Supreme Court podcast hosted by Will Baude and Dan Epps.

With arguments over the Second Amendment and the Excessive Fines Clause on the near horizon, this column seeks to provide some tranquil and more generalized ideas – a moment of Thanksgiving holiday respite. Whether you are a Supreme Court follower who usually shunts criminal law to the side, or an experienced criminal law reader who might enjoy some holiday dinner thoughts for your friends and family, this column seeks to demonstrate that much of criminal law is actually constitutional law – and perhaps show why that can be so interesting. To do so, I will scatter some examples from last term, drawn from my recently published Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term, Criminal Cases booklet. When explaining criminal law to your friends or just opining over Thanksgiving dinner, I’d like to show why your mantra should be “crim law is con law” and vice versa.

Winship – criminal law fundamentals are constitutional law

Every criminal law class I have taught over 40 years, from 1L first semester through advanced criminal procedure or federal criminal law, has begun with the same case: 1970’s In re Winship. Even non-lawyers know from film and TV that the prosecution’s high burden for proof in a criminal case is beyond a reasonable doubt. But do they know that this is constitutionally required? And perhaps more interesting, that this standard is nowhere, textually, in that document?

“[T]he Due Process Clause protects the accused against conviction except upon proof beyond reasonable doubt of every fact necessary to constitute the crime with which he is charged,” wrote Justice William Brennan Jr. for the Winship court. If only all Supreme Court decisions had such clear and succinct rule statements.

But why is this the rule? It is not found either in the body of the Constitution or in the Bill of Rights, which was adopted soon after the Constitution and focused largely on criminal law protections. Winship‘s answer: because that standard “dates back at least from our early years as a Nation,” “[i]t is now accepted in common law jurisdictions,” it is expressed “in many opinions of this Court,” and it has “long been assumed” to be “constitutionally required.” Thus history, tradition, and precedent support it. Perhaps most fundamentally, a high standard of proof, harder to satisfy than in civil law cases, is essential to fundamental fairness for the public as well as individuals charged with crimes. It is “indispensable to command the respect and confidence of the community” as well as “every individual” exposed to imprisonment. Or, as Justice John Harlan II wrote in an influential concurrence, this standard is “bottomed on a fundamental value determination of our society that it is far worse to convict an innocent man than to let a guilty man go free.”

There are almost no crimes mentioned in the Constitution

This sometimes surprises 1L students (and others). But the goal of the Constitution was to (re)describe a system of government, and form “a more perfect Union” after the prior Articles of Confederation had proved unsatisfactory. It was not to write a criminal code. The states were then (and still are) the primary forum for criminal law.

So the Constitution defines only one crime, treason (in Article III, section 3). It mentions a few others, like “Bribery” (in Article II, section 4) and “Breach of the Peace” with a general reference to “Felony” (in Article I, section 6). And of course the Impeachment Clause (Article II section 4) mentions “high Crimes and Misdemeanors,” without definition. Again, states were expected to take care of the substantive definition and application of virtually all criminal law. (However, as I explained some years ago, the First Congress in 1790 did enact over two dozen federal crimes.)

Yet a large focus of the Bill of Rights is criminal procedure

Three years after the Constitution was drafted, the Bill of Rights focused on criminal law rights in at least four proposed amendments (the Fourth, Fifth, Sixth, and Eighth). I won’t list the multitude of rights captured there, but they form the bulk of all criminal procedure law school classes today. The right to be free from unreasonable governmental searches and compelled self-incrimination, and the rights to counsel, jury trials, and no cruel and unusual punishments – and much more – are all embodied in the Bill of Rights.

One example from last term: in Villareal v. Texas, the court had to interpret the Sixth Amendment right to “Assistance of Counsel” to decide (unanimously) that a criminal trial judge can order that the defendant not discuss their ongoing testimony with their attorney during an overnight recess.

Why was the Bill of Rights so focused on criminal procedure rights? It’s a fun question to ask students, or at the Thanksgiving table if things get slow. Sooner or later someone gives the soundbite answer: “because most of the constitution’s framers were crooks.” They were certainly guilty of treason – then and still today a capital (that is, death penalty) offense, as well as other crimes (violence, destruction of property, incitement, and more). Had the revolutionary Framers been captured by the government (the British) they likely would have been hung. Instead, during the course of the revolution, numbers had been tried in absentia, found guilty by officials (not juries), and had their houses searched and occupied by troops. Cruel and unusual torture had been inflicted on some captured compatriots. When constitutional ratifying conventions demanded a bill of rights, protections from unfair criminal processes were therefore topmost on the minds of many drafters (if not perhaps “the People” at the time).

(Another aside: ask your lawyer friends to compare the content of civil procedure versus criminal procedure classes today. The latter full-semester course is almost entirely constitutional law – I used to call my own crim pro class “Con Law Three.” By contrast, civil procedure classes, also a full semester, focus largely on the nitty-gritty details of federal rules, only occasionally wandering into statutes or the Constitution.)

In addition to the four explicitly criminal-focused amendments, you might then add general constitutional ideas that are bound to capture some criminal law cases: the First, Second, Third, and Ninth Amendments. The First Amendment’s direction, that “Congress shall make no law” regarding (“respecting”) or abridging freedoms of religion, speech, and the press, is a constitutional law command against criminal laws as well as civil. So too is a protection of a right to keep and bear arms, and to not have government troops quartered in “any” house (not just your own).

And then consider the “great generalities” of the Constitution

In his 1921 Storrs Lectures at Yale Law School (subsequently published as “The Nature of the Judicial Process”), future Supreme Court Justice (and then New York Court of Appeals Judge) Benjamin Cardozo discussed “the great generalities of the Constitution.” Among these, the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses of the 14th Amendment are huge sources of criminal law doctrine. Just last term, for example, the procedural steps required to apply the Equal Protection Clause against racial (and other) bias in jury selection, and the idea that due process and judicial integrity requires a “miscarriage of justice” exception to guilty plea waivers, received focused Supreme Court attention (in Pitchford v. Cain and Hunter v. United States, respectively).

Criminal law cases focused on the meaning and application of these broad constitutional requirements arise regularly almost every Supreme Court term. Indeed, as I advise my students every year (again I aspire to teach with a smile, not didactic cynicism): no matter what arguments you make on the defense side of a criminal case, always add the words “and in violation of due process” to preserve at least a thread of a constitutional argument that you may not even perceive at the moment.

In addition to equal protection and due process, I (and others) would add the Ninth Amendment, which speaks of unspecified “rights … retained by the people.” Justices have sometimes suggested that the Ninth and Tenth Amendments state nothing but “truism[s],” while other Supreme Court decisions have relied (at least in part) on the Ninth. For some, invocation of the Ninth Amendment may provoke if not laughter (it having been referred to by one academic as a “constitutional jester”), then a distinctly conservative or “originalist” rejection. Yet other conservative scholars such as John Yoo and Calvin Massey (my late former colleague) have written expansively about it. As Randy Barnett has argued, the Ninth Amendment “means what it says,” and is “a significant guarantee of individual liberty.” If that is so, then it is (or could be) another source of criminal law protection for criminal defendants.

So criminal law is, very often, constitutional law

Thus it should be unsurprising (as detailed in my Annual Review of the Supreme Court’s Term, Criminal Law booklet) that 22 of the court’s merits decisions last term that address criminal law involved elements of constitutional law (17 fully argued cases plus five summary (unargued) decisions). That’s a substantial percentage of the court’s entire merits opinions docket, roughly a quarter or more.

Statutory criminal law cases also often involve constitutional law

By now I hope that you are persuaded: criminal law is (often) constitutional law. “But wait – there’s more!” When you combine the Constitution’s Supremacy Clause with the oft-cited judicial doctrine of constitutional avoidance, criminal cases requiring statutory interpretation also fall into this category. That is, these are criminal law cases that involve consideration of constitutional law. Advocates in statutory cases often raise potential constitutional objections to a criminal statute or to its application in their case, or they may raise constitutional law ideas in favor of their preferred interpretation. In addition, an understanding of constitutional doctrine can be necessary to properly evaluate the merits of a statutory claim. The bottom line is that, in many statutory criminal cases, explication or consideration of constitutional law is necessary or helpful to explain the result.

Just a few examples from last term: In Barrett v. United States, the court had to mine the details of double jeopardy doctrine to agree, unanimously, that a statute could be interpreted as not permitting two convictions for a single act, thereby avoiding a constitutional problem. In Olivier v. City of Brandon, the court had to examine Olivier’s constitutional claims in order to decide whether the federal civil rights statutes were a proper vehicle for him to sue under. And in Whitton v. Dixon, the court had to briefly explain the constitutional Giglio doctrine, regarding a prosecutor’s failure to disclose exculpatory impeachment information, to reverse an application of the federal habeas corpus statue.

Immigration cases also often require constitutional law, either to dispose of the merits or to resolve statutory issues in them. Last term’s birthright citizenship case, Trump v. Barbara, is the most obvious example. Because immigration and criminal law cases are often intertwined – consider recent ICE arrests, detentions, and criminal violation grounds for removal – I include them in my annual review as well as the purview of this column. And even civil cases that I consider related to criminal law often require consideration of constitutional law concepts. For example, last term’s Hencely v. Fluor Corp., rejecting a claim of government contractor immunity, required consideration of constitutional preemption doctrine.

In other words, criminal law mixed with constitutional law is everywhere.

Last week, many of us were focused on the details of elections around the country, big and small. And next week, after Thanksgiving, will be chock full of criminal law and related Supreme Court oral arguments. So I’ve tried to give you a break today, and provide a few thoughts that are, perhaps, entertaining, or provocative, or at least interesting ways to navigate your mealtime gatherings (rather than focusing on the usual subjects). For some of you, perhaps this column has simply demonstrated what you already considered obvious; or perhaps it has opened interesting linkages in your mind between constitutional law and criminal law. In any case, thanks for reading this far. Next week I hope you are fortunate enough to breathe relaxing breaths, give thanks, and dwell not on legal minutiae but on what really matters.

Rory Little has been teaching Constitutional and Criminal Law topics at UC Law SF (formerly Hastings) for over 30 years, after 12 years of practice.

Recommended Citation: Rory Little, Criminal law is constitutional law, SCOTUSblog (Nov. 20, 2026, 10:00 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/11/criminal-law-is-constitutional-law/

#7518. Law firm apologizes to truckers for ‘serial killer’ ad

A Texas law firm is apologizing for an ad in Maxim magazine that created such an outcry among truckers that truck stops pulled the publication from their shelves.

The full-page ad for San Antonio law firm Villarreal & Begum showed a picture of a truck cab beneath the words “serial killer.” Both the law firm and Maxim are apologizing for the ad after Pilot Flying J and TravelCenters of America pulled the magazine from their shelves. Publications with stories include HDT Trucking Info, TheTrucker.com, CSPNet.com, KIROTV.com and LandLinemag.com.

The copy read: “3,561 people died on America’s highways last year. Another 2.36 million were injured. You need a law firm you can Trust. You need Experience. You need Strength. You need Villarreal & Begum. We’re proven leaders in prosecuting cases involving death and catastrophic injury.”

In its statement, the law firm says it never intended “to disparage the hardworking Americans that drive tractor-trailers for a living. Our intent was to reach out to those individuals who have been involved in catastrophic accidents as a result of irresponsible drivers. The ad was inartfully created, and we could see how it may have caused our message to be misconstrued. We recognize the service that truck drivers provide to this nation and acknowledge that most truck drivers are safe and responsible drivers.”

Maxim also issued a statement saying the ad “does not reflect the beliefs or opinions of the people at this magazine, which recently has begun operating under new ownership.” The ad has been pulled from Maxim’s digital copy and replaced with facts about the trucking industry.
